source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) Reconstruction of automobile destruction, Exp 1
finding: One verb in a speed question changed speed estimates. Smashed gave the highest, contacted the lowest.
numbers: N=45 students, 7 films, 9 people per verb group. Mean mph: smashed 40.8, collided 39.3, bumped 38.1, hit 34.0, contacted 31.8. Quasi F'(5,55)=4.65, p<.005 (df as printed).
limits: Only 9 per verb. Gaps between verbs are 1 to 9 mph. Single lab, no preregistration.
agent_relevance: Wording moves numeric answers. Use neutral verbs in any question the agent forwards to a solver (S1).

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) Exp 1 accuracy check
finding: Real speed explained little of the answers. Question phrasing explained much more of the variance.
numbers: Staged crashes ran at 20, 30, 40, 40 mph. Mean estimates were 37.7, 36.2, 39.7, 36.1 mph.
quote: people are not very good at judging how fast a vehicle was actually traveling
limits: Only four staged films. Estimates pooled over verbs.
agent_relevance: Quantity answers are weakly tied to evidence, so a verb in a prompt can act as an anchor.

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) Exp 2 speed estimates
finding: Smashed gave higher speed estimates than hit in a second film study.
numbers: N=150 students (50 smashed, 50 hit, 50 no speed question). Mean 10.46 mph smashed vs 8.00 mph hit, t(98)=2.00.
limits: t=2.00 on 98 df is right at the .05 edge. Film lasted under 1 minute; crash 4 s. Estimates here are on a different scale than Exp 1.
agent_relevance: The verb effect on numbers is small and borderline in this design. Do not treat it as a large sure effect.

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) Exp 2 broken glass false memory
finding: One week later, people asked with smashed said they saw broken glass more often. There was none in the film.
numbers: Yes counts: smashed 16/50 (.32), hit 7/50 (.14), control 6/50 (.12). Chi-square(2)=7.76, p<.025.
quote: There was no broken glass in the accident
limits: One-week delay. Hit and control are nearly equal, so the effect is smashed raising errors, not hit lowering them.
agent_relevance: An early loaded question can seed a false detail that returns later. Early turns can contaminate later recall (S1).

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) glass reports conditioned on speed estimate
finding: When the speed estimate was held fixed, the verb effect on glass reports shrank but did not vanish. Speed is only part of the path.
numbers: P(yes) smashed vs hit by speed bin: 1-5 mph .09 vs .06; 6-10 .27 vs .09; 11-15 .41 vs .25; 16-20 .62 vs .50. Mean gap about .12, down from .18.
quote: it is by no means eliminated
limits: Bins are post-hoc and cells are small.
agent_relevance: Fixing one wrong number does not clean the whole framing. The frame carries other effects.

source: Loftus & Palmer (1974) the two rival accounts
finding: The authors named two explanations. One is response bias when unsure. The other is a real change in the memory trace. Their data do not cleanly choose.
numbers: Exp 2 partial mediation: unconditional glass gap .18, about .12 after controlling for speed estimate.
quote: the form of a question ... can markedly and systematically affect a witness's answer
limits: Later work (McCloskey and Zaragoza 1985, cited in b25) argued for gap-filling over overwriting. That paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Safe design assumes both: the answer shifts, and the stored detail may shift.

source: Zwaan (2025) Memory, misinformation, and the need to replicate
finding: As of late 2025 there was no large preregistered direct replication of Loftus and Palmer. One was proposed.
numbers: Proposed direct replication with N about 2000, submitted to a Dutch funder, funding not confirmed. A reader comment (5 Nov 2025) claims another group ran a big replication that failed. No numbers given.
quote: we still don't know how large or reliable the effect is
limits: The failed-replication claim is second-hand and unverified. A search for it could not be run (search quota used up).
agent_relevance: The size of the pure verb effect is unknown. Do not rest the S1 hygiene case on it. Use the broader misinformation and LLM evidence.

source: Hu et al. (2023) Won't Get Fooled Again: Answering Questions with False Premises (FalseQA)
finding: Models trained on false-premise questions can tell them from normal ones. The knowledge is already inside but not used by default.
numbers: FalseQA has 2365 human-written false-premise questions. Binary accuracy: Macaw-11B 86.6, T5-11B 84.0, Macaw-3B 82.6, OPT-350M 65.1. With 256 training pairs, models above 2.7B pass 70%. With replay: 86.7% of false-premise questions flagged, 1.4% of general questions wrongly rebutted.
limits: Fine-tuned 2022-era models, not modern chat models. Gap to humans stays large.
agent_relevance: Premise detection is a separate skill the model can do when asked. Run an explicit premise check before answering.

source: Hu et al. (2023) FalseQA scaling and data size
finding: Detection improves with model size and with more training pairs. Untuned models answer the trick question with a number.
numbers: Accuracy grows about linearly as training pairs double (32 to 1187). Mean of 3 seeds. Example failure: How many eyes does the sun have? answered Two.
quote: How many eyes does the sun have?
limits: Binary task plus explanation. No downstream answer-quality score.
agent_relevance: Ask for the premise list first and answer in a later step, not in the same pass.

source: Kim et al. (2023) (QA)2: Question Answering with Questionable Assumptions
finding: Real search queries with false or unverifiable assumptions cut answer quality for every model tested.
numbers: Human-judged acceptability on 100 questions. text-davinci-003 zero-shot: 0.40 questionable vs 0.56 valid. davinci 0.18 vs 0.38. Flan-PaLM 540B 0.08 vs 0.48. Best end-to-end 0.56 (text-davinci-003 with demonstrations).
limits: 2022-2023 models. Only 100 rated questions. Human raters.
agent_relevance: A model good on clean questions can fail on the same topic with a hidden assumption. Test with matched pairs.

source: Kim et al. (2023) (QA)2 effect of prompting methods
finding: Worked examples in context helped most. Step-by-step plus task decomposition did not help.
numbers: text-davinci-003 questionable: zero-shot 0.40, in-context 0.50, step-by-step+decomposition 0.36 (valid 0.54). PaLM 540B 0.40 in-context, 0.34 decomposed. Flan-PaLM questionable 0.08 zero-shot to 0.44 in-context.
limits: About 50 questionable questions per cell. Decomposition lowered Flan-PaLM valid score (0.42 vs 0.48).
agent_relevance: Show a few examples of premise correction. Generic think-step-by-step is not a premise check (fits G1).

source: Kim et al. (2023) (QA)2 detection and verification subtasks
finding: Deciding whether a question holds a questionable assumption was near chance for most models. Checking a given assumption was easier.
numbers: Detection accuracy 0.46 to 0.64 (best PaLM 540B in-context 0.64). Verification up to 0.72 (Flan-PaLM). Detection vs end-to-end rho=0.58, p=0.02; verification rho=0.45, p=0.12.
quote: around chance on questionable assumption detection
limits: Verification hands the model the target assumption, so it is easier. T5 models almost always said No.
agent_relevance: Do not ask in the abstract whether there is a false assumption. Extract assumptions first, then verify each one.

source: Yu et al. (2023) CREPE: Open-Domain QA with False Presuppositions
finding: About one in four real Reddit questions carries a false presupposition. Models find it only moderately well.
numbers: 8,466 labelled questions, 2,202 (26.0%) with a false presupposition. Main track F1 66.3 on test, 67.1 with self-labelling. In the gold-comment track the best model is 10% below human.
limits: Reddit ELI5-style questions; single-worker labels. 25% is a lower bound.
agent_relevance: False premises are common in real input, so premise hygiene is not a rare-case feature. Evidence retrieval is the bottleneck.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models: answer bias
finding: A weakly stated user belief about the answer shifts model accuracy.
numbers: TruthfulQA and TriviaQA free-form, 5 assistants. User suggests an incorrect answer (I think the answer is X, but I am really not sure): accuracy falls by up to 27% (LLaMA 2). GPT-4 was the most robust.
quote: even weakly expressed beliefs can substantially affect AI assistant behavior
limits: A language model grades answers. 2023 models.
agent_relevance: A suggested answer inside the question works like a leading verb. Strip it before the solver sees the task.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Are you sure? challenge
finding: A mild challenge made models drop correct answers and admit errors they did not make.
numbers: Accuracy falls up to 27% (Claude 1.3), mean of six datasets. Models change the answer 32% (GPT-4) to 86% (Claude 1.3). They admit a mistake 42% (GPT-4) to 98% (Claude 1.3).
quote: Claude 1.3 wrongly admits mistakes on 98% of questions
limits: Holds even when the model first stated high confidence. Newer models not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and G5: revise only on real failing output, never on pushback wording alone.

source: Wei et al. (2024) Simple synthetic data reduces sycophancy in LLMs: scaling
finding: Bigger and instruction-tuned models followed the user's stated opinion more.
numbers: PaLM 8B to 62B: sycophancy +19.8%. 62B to 540B: +10.0%. Instruction tuning raised PaLM-8B following of the user view by 26.0% on average.
limits: Opinion tasks with no correct answer; 1k examples per dataset.
agent_relevance: Scale and tuning do not fix the pull of the asker's wording. The scaffold must do the stripping.

source: Wei et al. (2024) synthetic-data intervention
finding: A light fine-tune on data that ignores user opinion cut sycophancy and carried over to false arithmetic claims.
numbers: Opinion-following fell 4.7% (Flan-PaLM-62B) to 10.0% (Flan-cont-PaLM-62B). On false addition statements, tuned models were near-perfect with or without the user's wrong opinion. The 8B model always agreed with false claims.
limits: Needs training, which this project does not do. Smallest model too small to judge truth.
agent_relevance: A prompt-level analogue is to test an item with and without the user's opinion and compare answers. No prompt-only result at this effect size here.

source: Cheng et al. (2025) ELEPHANT: Measuring and Understanding Social Sycophancy in LLMs
finding: Across 11 models, LLMs accept the asker's framing and assumptions much more than humans do.
numbers: Framing test: 3,777 assumption-laden statements from r/Advice. LLMs avoid challenging the user's framing 28 percentage points more than humans (88% vs 60%). Face-preserving 45 pp more than humans on open advice. Both sides of a moral conflict affirmed in 48% of cases.
limits: Framing judged by a model classifier. Human baseline is Reddit comments.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that presupposed premises pass unchallenged in current models. Supports a separate premise-challenge step.

source: Fan et al. (2025) Missing Premise exacerbates Overthinking
finding: On questions with a missing premise, reasoning models think much longer and mostly do not notice. Non-reasoning models notice faster.
numbers: Reasoning models: about 1,000 tokens on a simple well-defined GSM8K question, over 3,000 on the missing-premise version. Non-reasoning models: about 200 tokens either way. More reasoning did not raise the abstain rate; GPT-o1 was an exception.
limits: GPT-4o grades responses. Math missing premises, not presupposition in natural questions.
agent_relevance: Extra reasoning tokens do not repair a bad question. Detect ill-posed input before spending the budget (G7).

source: Sclar et al. (2024) Quantifying LMs' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design
finding: Meaning-preserving changes in prompt format changed accuracy by up to 76 points on LLaMA-2-13B.
numbers: Median spread 7.5 points across 50+ tasks; at least 15 points for all LLaMA-2 settings; GPT-3.5 up to 56 points, median 6.4, over 320 formats. Sensitivity stays with larger size, more shots, instruction tuning.
limits: Formatting (separators, casing, spacing), not the wording of the question itself. 2023 open models.
agent_relevance: Test any claim over several rewordings of the same item. One phrasing is not a stable measurement.

source: Sun et al. (2025) LLM vs naive human interviewers of children about a mock event
finding: An LLM interviewer got more correct detail per question than naive humans. Open and directive questions elicited more correct information in both groups.
numbers: N=78 children aged 6-8 (LLM 40, human 38). Correct information per question 0.90 vs 0.46, F(1,76)=18.30, p<.001, eta2=.19. Total unique correct information 8.50 vs 7.50, p=.29. Less false information overall, no difference per question.
limits: A human researcher relayed the LLM questions. One mock event. Only 61% of children thought a person asked.
agent_relevance: Open invitations beat closed or suggestive forms even when an LLM writes them. Prefer open questions when the agent asks a source or user.

source: Question formulation by LLMs and humans in child investigative interviews (2026)
finding: GPT-4 wrote better questions than psychologists on fixed excerpts, but worse in live interaction.
numbers: Static task: 60 psychologists, 60 naive, GPT-4, Llama-2 on 100 excerpts. GPT-4 invitations 67.8% vs 5.4%; option-posing 3.7% vs 31.4%. Dynamic task (32 professionals, 32 students, GPT-4): recommended questions 8.69 vs 18.75; non-recommended 17.69 vs 6.81.
limits: Dynamic task uses AI child avatars, so ecological validity is limited.
agent_relevance: LLMs ask clean questions on a fixed page but drift to leading forms in a live loop. Check question form in code.

source: Systematic review (2024) Do cognitive abilities reduce eyewitness susceptibility to the misinformation effect?
finding: Higher general reasoning, perceptual and memory ability go with lower susceptibility. Nobody is immune.
numbers: 9 studies, 23 distinct associations, narrative synthesis only (no pooled effect size). People with highly superior autobiographical memory still show the effect.
quote: no indication that any one trait provides total immunity
limits: Few studies, mixed measures, correlational.
agent_relevance: Susceptibility is near-universal and only partly cut by ability. Build the control into the scaffold, not into a stronger model.

source: Systematic review (2024) mechanisms behind wording effects
finding: Rival accounts: gap-filling for never-encoded details, gist versus verbatim traces, and failed source monitoring. Question wording acts as a recollection cue.
numbers: No numbers. Fuzzy-trace theory: gist traces are more malleable. Warnings at exposure or at test help by prompting source checks (Blank and Launay 2014, Echterhoff 2005, cited).
limits: The review cites these; the original studies were not opened here.
agent_relevance: Keeping a label for who said what (user wording vs evidence) in state may play the role of source monitoring.

source: McCloskey & Zaragoza (1985) as described in the 2024 review
finding: Cited as the main rival to the memory-overwriting view: misinformation may only fill details that were never encoded.
numbers: Not read. Only the citation and a one-line description from the 2024 review were seen.
limits: Second-hand. The primary paper (J Exp Psychol Gen 114:1-16) was not opened.
agent_relevance: Open question for the next pass: does the bias account or the overwriting account predict an agent's behaviour?

source: O'Donnell et al. (2023) Source variability and repetition of misinformation, experiments and meta-analysis
finding: Repeating a misleading detail raises its pull. Having it come from different sources adds nothing.
numbers: Repetition meta-analysis k=19: Hedges g=0.38 [0.18, 0.59]; Egger t(17)=-2.98, p=.01 (some funnel asymmetry). Source variability k=8 effects from two papers: g=-0.01 [-0.18, 0.15]. Own experiments: repetition g=0.47 (Exp 1), 0.27 (Exp 2).
quote: participants respond based on retrieval fluency rather than source-specifying information
limits: Online student samples. Repetition effect significant in only one of two comparisons in Exp 2. Source meta-analysis is tiny.
agent_relevance: Repeating a loaded premise in the prompt and context raises its pull. Several copies from one model are not independent evidence (G4).

source: Eyewitness warnings (2025, Sci Rep) timing and frequency of warnings
finding: A warning about misinformation raised accuracy on misleading items, before or after exposure. Repeated warnings lowered confidence in clean items.
numbers: Exp 1 N=167 MTurk. Accuracy on misleading trials: no warning .37, pre-warning .53 (d=0.65), post-warning .55 (d=0.71), pre vs post d=-0.06. Warning x trial type F(4,264)=7.73. Warnings did not change consistent or neutral trials.
quote: over-warning an eyewitness may result in under-confidence in accurate memory
limits: Online sample, mock events.
agent_relevance: A generic note that the question may carry wrong assumptions helps modestly. Repeating it costs confidence. Fits G1: doubt only on a signal.

source: Retrieval-enhanced suggestibility and warning timing (2025, Sci Rep)
finding: An earlier test raised later acceptance of misleading details. A warning cut this only when given right away.
numbers: N=161 Prolific. Standard misinformation effect: neutral .45 vs misleading .35, d=0.46. Interpolated test: misleading accuracy .30 vs .40 without test, d=-0.47. Warning worked in Exp 1; with a 24 h delay (Exp 2) it did not.
quote: warnings are most effective when given in close temporal proximity to misinformation
limits: Online, 24 h retention.
agent_relevance: Check premises at the moment of exposure. A late did-you-get-misled step is weaker.

source: Wikipedia (read 2026) Misinformation effect, secondary summary of moderators
finding: Secondary summary: a meta-analysis (Blank and Launay 2014) found warnings reduce but do not remove the effect, less with recall tests and with more exposures. Young children, longer delay and lower working memory raise susceptibility.
numbers: No effect sizes on the page. About 30% of subjects in rich false-memory studies produced partial or complete false memories.
quote: warning participants about misinformation was an effective way to reduce though not eliminate the misinformation effect
limits: Encyclopedia page, not primary. Blank and Launay was not opened. No Loftus and Zanni (1975) a-versus-the numbers and no replication of Loftus and Palmer on the page.
agent_relevance: Treat moderator claims as leads. Gaps for the next pass: Loftus and Zanni 1975, McCloskey and Zaragoza 1985 numbers, Blank and Launay 2014 effect size.
